title: Password Strength Checker (Private, Offline)
description: Check how strong a password is with zxcvbn: score, estimated crack times, warnings and tips. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent or stored.
quickAnswer: Type a password to see a strength score from 0 (very weak) to 4 (very strong), how long an attacker would need to guess it, and what makes it weak. The check uses zxcvbn-ts, which looks for common passwords, words, names, keyboard patterns, dates and substitutions like 0 for o, and runs entirely on your device. Long, unique passphrases score best; 'password' scores 0.

formula.title: How Strength Is Estimated
formula.expression: Score = f(log10 guesses)   ·   guesses = the fewest guesses an attacker needs, using dictionaries, patterns and brute force
formula.explanation: zxcvbn splits the password into pieces it recognises: dictionary words and common passwords (also when misspelled or written with substitutions like 4 for a), names, dates, repeats, sequences such as abc or 123, and keyboard walks such as qwerty. It finds the cheapest combination of those pieces and counts how many guesses a cracker following that strategy would need. Fewer than 1,000 guesses scores 0, fewer than a million 1, fewer than 100 million 2, fewer than 10 billion 3, and anything more 4. Crack times divide the guesses by attack speeds: 100 guesses per hour for an online login with rate limiting, and 10 billion per second for an offline attack on a fast, unsalted hash.

commonMistakes.title: Relying on character substitutions
commonMistakes.description: P@ssw0rd is still 'password' to a cracker: tools try common substitutions automatically. Length and unpredictability matter far more than swapping letters for symbols.

commonMistakes.title: Reusing a strong password
commonMistakes.description: If one site leaks your password, attackers try it everywhere else (credential stuffing). Even a very strong password is unsafe if it is used on more than one site. A password manager makes unique passwords easy.

commonMistakes.title: Adding a year or number at the end
commonMistakes.description: Summer2026 or Password1! follow patterns cracking rules try first. Predictable endings add very little strength.

commonMistakes.title: Pasting your real password into websites
commonMistakes.description: Only check passwords in tools that run locally, like this one, which does not send what you type anywhere. Better still, check a password that is similar in style rather than the exact one you use.

commonMistakes.title: Changing passwords on a schedule
commonMistakes.description: NIST no longer recommends forced periodic changes, because people respond with predictable tweaks. Change a password when there is a sign it has been exposed.

faqs.a: Type it into the box. You will see a score from 0 to 4, estimated crack times for online and offline attacks, and specific warnings, such as 'this is a common password' or 'dates are easy to guess'.

faqs.q: Is it safe to type my password here?
faqs.a: The check runs entirely in your browser, in a background worker on this page. The password is not sent, stored, logged or put in the page address, and the field is cleared when you leave. If you prefer, test a password that is similar in style instead of your real one.

Length and unpredictability. A random password of 15 or more characters, or a passphrase of several unrelated words, is strong. Common words, names, dates, keyboard patterns and simple substitutions make it weak.

faqs.q: How long should a password be?
faqs.a: NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires at least 15 characters for passwords used on their own and at least 8 when combined with another factor, and recommends allowing at least 64 characters. Longer is better.

faqs.q: Are password complexity rules still recommended?
faqs.a: No. NIST says services should not require mixtures of character types, and should instead block common and compromised passwords and allow long passphrases.
An open-source password strength estimator first released by Dropbox. This tool uses zxcvbn-ts, a maintained TypeScript version, with its English and common-password dictionaries hosted on this site.

faqs.q: How is the crack time calculated?
faqs.a: The estimated number of guesses is divided by an attack speed: 100 guesses per hour for a rate-limited online login and 10 billion per second for an offline attack on a fast hash. Real attacks vary, so treat the times as a guide.

faqs.q: How do I make a strong password I can remember?
faqs.a: Use a passphrase of four or more random, unrelated words, or let a password manager or the ToolsBuilt password generator create and store a random password for you.

what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.heading: What NIST Says About Passwords, in Plain Words
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.p1: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes the guidance many organisations follow, SP 800-63B. Its current revision (SP 800-63B-4) turned years of research into a few clear rules for services that set password policies:
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.li1: Length over complexity: a password used on its own must be at least 15 characters (at least 8 if it is one part of multi-factor login), and services should allow at least 64 characters.
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.li2: No composition rules: services should not force mixtures like "one upper case, one number, one symbol"; those rules produce predictable passwords such as Password1!.
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.li3: Block bad passwords: new passwords must be checked against a list of common, expected and previously breached passwords, and rejected if they appear.
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.li4: No forced periodic changes: services should not make people change passwords on a schedule, but must force a change when there is evidence a password has been compromised.
what-nist-says-about-passwords-in.li5: Allow every character: spaces and all printable characters should be accepted, which makes passphrases practical, and pasting from password managers should be allowed.

score-guide.heading: Score Guide
score-guide.td3: Among the first passwords any attacker tries
score-guide.td6: Protects only against a heavily rate-limited online attack
score-guide.td9: Survives an online attack but falls quickly offline
score-guide.td12: Resists offline attacks on slow, salted hashes
score-guide.td15: Resists offline attacks even on fast hashes
score-guide.p1: The estimate cannot know whether a password has leaked in a data breach or is used on other sites, so a high score is necessary but not sufficient. Use a unique password for every account, turn on multi-factor authentication where you can, and let a password manager remember them.
